content: If we declare that IdealLeanTT is extensional, then we can prove (propositionally) that the auxilliary translation for nested inductive types satisfies all the iota rules necessary (and then reflect this definitionally). We don't use the reflection rule otherwise. This is probably a stupid idea, but it doesn't increase logical strength does it?

E.g. given

inductive Sexp (α : Type u)
  | atom : α → Sexp α
  | list : List (Sexp α) → Sexp α

generate AuxSexp and ListSexp as usual, then set def Sexp := AuxSexp, def Sexp.atom := ..., def Sexp.rec := ... and so on, ensuring AuxSexp and ListSexp do not appear in the type signatures. Then prove the iota rules propositionally, corollary definitionally, and then seal off Sexp making them irreducible, and retain only the fact that the iota rules hold.

Pros: same logical strength, don't have to theorise about nesteds, and the rest of the kernel doesn't have to change if you only care about soundness
Cons: you lose injectivity of type constructors, probably many more
If it walks and quacks like a nested inductive type...

You are not going insane, I have seen this being discussed a few times ind various variants. There is more than iota rules about inductives, though: projections, structure eta, unit-like eta (ok, most don’t apply to nested inductives). Then there is the question if we pay more than we get if we allow sealing and using prop eqs as definitional equalities, I hear many nice metatheoretical properties get lost. And finally, once you take this step, why stop here? IdealLeanTT could just have non-mutual inductives and you elaborate the mutual ones. Or it could have no user-defined inductives at all, but W-types or something like that, and all inductives are translated.

I find this an very interesting direction and hope someone explores this. And it doesn’t have to be “lean has to change its elaborator and kernel”, it could be a “here is a lean checker that translates to this other theory, and here is a checker for that theory” and it would already be useful as an external checker.

FWIW I believe this is the way to go to explain the fancy features of real proof assistants: a very expressive kernel (with eg mutual nested inductive types) + a verified-in-theory translation to a simpler type theory. This gives a nice, gradual way to explain the fancy features away, without people having to understand any model construction.

Of course, at the end of the day it is also nice to build a model of the simpler type theory to which we have reduced the fancy features. But I believe that explaining the fancy features that people don't usually think about on paper in terms of simpler ones is much more important in terms of trust/soundness than to formally verify a set-theoretic model of, say, CIC with only W types, which is something that is well studied and well understood.
